finding.claim: The caller's identity is read directly from the X-Session-User-Verified request header, which the client controls. The name suggests a trusted proxy sets it, but this code does not check that. An attacker can send any user ID and inherit that user's grants on rename (write) and delete (delete). This is conditional on deployment: if a proxy always overwrites or strips this header, the risk is reduced, but nothing in this code enforces that.
finding.sink: Grant lookup resource['grants'][user] in acl.is_allowed (acl.py:5), reached via ensure_allowed for rename (views.py:26-27) and is_allowed for delete (views.py:18-19)

Same identity flows into the delete path (also broken by F1)

finding.guards_checked: No signature, session, or cryptographic verification of the header. No check that the request came from a trusted proxy. No IP or origin restriction. The default-deny for a missing header (grants.get(None, []) returns []) only blocks anonymous callers, not impersonation of a listed user. The rename authorization check itself (acl.py:8-10 abort 403) works correctly once g.user is set.

verdict.guard_found: none. views.py:12 sets g.user from the raw header with no verification. The only check on the rename path is acl.py:9-10 (ensure_allowed → abort 403), which trusts that identity. Nothing in the code checks a proxy, signature, or session.
verdict.reason: The rename impersonation chain holds: views.py:12 takes g.user from the client-controlled header, acl.py:5 looks up grants by that value, and views.py:27 writes the name after ensure_allowed passes, so any caller who sends a granted user's ID can rename. The delete sub-claim is misdescribed, though: views.py:18 calls require_allowed (is_allowed, a bool-returning function) as a bare statement and discards the result, so delete is not gated by identity at all, and spoofing is not what enables it.
